paper_title: Coding4Games: Can Modern Coding Agents Play Modern Video Games?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Games, especially modern AAA games, challenge language models to perceive complex scenes, control actions, and make decisions over long horizons. Existing game benchmarks primarily test language models as computer-use agents that query a language model throughout play, incurring repeated inference cost and, in real-time games, acting while the environment continues to evolve. We ask whether coding agents can learn from game interaction to develop standalone game-playing programs that run without language model inference. We thus introduce Coding4Games, a benchmark for evaluating whether coding agents can develop standalone programs that play modern games through visual observations and standard game inputs. Coding4Games has three defining features: 1) Diverse Modern Games, covering 15 games with diverse visual, strategic, and control demands; 2) Development-Test Separation, in which a coding agent uses a sandbox and the standard player interface to iteratively develop a program, after which the selected program is frozen and independently tested without language-model inference; and 3) Outcome and Process Evaluation, which measures not only game performance and reliability but also how agents use feedback, revise programs, and resolve problems during development. Across 15 games, the best program per game outscores the strongest GUI baseline on 13 and ties it on one. The human player outscores all agents on 10 games. We additionally examine the effects of development budgets. Coding4Games evaluates whether coding agents can turn their understanding of complex interactive environments into programs that work reliably on their own.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Coding agents can autonomously tackle wide range of software tasks (Jimenez et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Merrill et al., 2026; OpenAI, 2025; Anthropic, 2025). Yet existing evaluations primarily focus on conventional software tasks, leaving their ability to develop programs for complex, dynamic environments less explored. Modern video games present such challenges: their rich visual interfaces, large state and action spaces, and real-time dynamics require programs that integrate perception, strategic decision-making, and precise control. Developing such programs requires agents to understand game rules and iteratively debug behavior through interaction, making modern games demanding testbed for evaluating coding agents. However, existing game benchmarks largely evaluate direct gameplay rather than the development of standalone game-playing programs. They typically adopt computer-use setting,i.e., GUI Agent, in which language model repeatedly observes the game and selects the next action (Fig. 1(a)) (Paglieri et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Park et al., 2026; Ouyang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b). This requires repeated model inference during play; in real-time games, the environment may continue to evolve during model inferences (Zhang et al., 2025; Ouyang et al., 2026). complementary line of work studies API-based game-playing programs, which receive structured game states and issue actions through programmatic interfaces. CodeClash (Yang et al., 2026) and ProxyWar (Peng et al., 2026) ask coding agents to write and iteratively revise bots that compete in game arenas, and related work optimizes game policies or world models represented as code (Kuang et al., 2025; Bachrach et al., 2025; Lehrach et al., 2026). However, game-specific APIs expose structured state and action abstractions that bypass the perception and low-level control required in real games, limiting applicability to and transfer across modern titles (Tab. 1). We bring these two lines of work together and ask: Can general coding agent understand modern game through visual interaction and write program that plays it using only standard game controls, without access to game-specific APIs? We define game-playing program as an executable program built with general-purpose libraries, whose logic maps visual observations to control actions without language-model inference during play, as shown in Fig. 1 (b). Once developed, such program runs without further language-model calls, while its behavior can be inspected, rerun, and systematically tested. This setting evaluates whether coding agents can translate game understanding into reliable executable behavior. To answer this question, we introduce Coding4Games, benchmark with three defining features. 1) Diverse Modern Games. Coding4Games evaluates 15 games spanning diverse visual, strategic, and control demands, rather than restricting evaluation to classic games with comparatively simple visual interfaces and control schemes. It covers games across five categories: Combat & Action Timing, 3D Sports & Precision Control, Movement & Timing, Strategy & Resource Planning, and Multi-step Task Execution. 2) DevelopmentTest Separation. During the Development stage, coding agents explore games, develop programs, and self-test in persistent sandbox, interacting with games through gym-like interface provided by the game server. During the Test stage, the selected program is frozen and evaluated in fresh environment without language-model inference, testing whether it can play reliably on its own. 3) Outcome and Process Evaluation. Beyond game performance, we assess how coding agents use execution feedback, revise programs, and test whether revisions resolve targeted problems. We further examine the correlation between the scores achieved in the coding agent and GUI agent settings using the same model. Our experiments with 12 coding agents demonstrate the potential to turn game interaction into standalone programs. The best program per game outscores the strongest GUI baseline on 13 of 15 games and ties it on one. The human player outscores all agents in 10 games, while the best program per game beats the human in three and ties in two. Process analysis further reveals that self-testing often fails to translate feedback into effective strategy revisions. Together, these findings highlight the promise of code as reusable representation of interactive behavior, while identifying strategy discovery and reliable improvement through interaction as central challenges for coding agents. In summary, our contributions are as follows: We formulate game playing by coding agents as the development of standalone programs through the standard player interface, with protocol that separates development from independent testing without language-model inference. sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Game Agents. Deep reinforcement learning and self-play have enabled strong game-playing policies in Atari, board games, and real-time strategy (Mnih et al., 2013; Silver et al., 2018; Vinyals et al., 2019), while learning from gameplay demonstrations supports instruction-conditioned and generalist policies (Baker et al., 2022; SIMA Team et al., 2024; Magne et al., 2026). Language-model agents interleave reasoning and action, revise plans after execution failures, and retain experience in memory (Yao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023, 2025). Systems such as Cradle and Voyager further organize behavior into executable skills that agents can compose and reuse (Tan et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024). The approaches closest to our setting use language models to revise Atari policies from execution traces, generate best-response programs against Checkers bots, or synthesize executable simulators for classical planning (Kuang et al., 2025; Bachrach et al., 2025; Lehrach et al., 2026). These approaches separate program construction from execution, allowing the resulting programs to run without per-action language-model inference. Building on this separation, Coding4Games independently tests the standalone game-playing programs produced by general coding agents. Benchmarks for Coding and Game Agents. Coding benchmarks differ in the scope of the artifact and the environment in which it is evaluated: programs satisfying inputoutput requirements (Chen et al., 2021; Austin et al., 2021; Hendrycks et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023; Jain et al., 2025), repository-level issue resolution and the interfaces through which agents edit and execute code (Jimenez et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Merrill et al., 2026), and interaction in heterogeneous environments, websites, desktops, and embodied control (Liu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2026). For games, From Code to Play, ProxyWar, and CodeClash are the closest precedents, evaluating program search, testing and repair, and repeated codebase editing under competition (Eberhardinger et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026). Coding agents also develop the games themselves, with methods for generation from specifications (Jiang et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026b) and refinement through playtesting (Huang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026), benchmarks for development (Chi et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026d; Lee et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026) and replication (Qiao et al., 2026), and generated environments for evaluating and training game agents (Aggarwal and Welleck, 2026; Liu et al., 2026). Game agent evaluation instead builds on established platforms (Bellemare et al., 2013; Kempka et al., 2016; Guss et al., 2019; Côté et al., 2019; Hausknecht et al., 2020) and recent language-model suites (Paglieri et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026; Park et al., 2026), whose conditions are essential to interpreting reported performance: real-time versus paused execution (Zhang et al., 2025), state-based verification (Ouyang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c) versus model-judged milestones (Zhang et al., 2026b), and improvement across attempts versus transfer to held-out variants (Lin et al., 2026). Self-Improving Agents. Self-improvement methods differ in what changes and what persists across tasks: program libraries learned together with search-guiding model (Ellis et al., 2023), parameters updated from accepted selfgenerated rationales (Zelikman et al., 2022), outputs or verbal feedback refined in context (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023), and reusable tools and skills accumulated with fixed language-model weights (Schick et al., 2023; Cai et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2026a). Closer to our setting, one line searches over executable policies and agent implementations (Kumar et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2025), and recursive variants additionally modify the improvement machinery itself (Zelikman et al., 2024; Yin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a)program-level modification that should be distinguished from changing the underlying model. Coding4Games evaluates the reliability and cost of the resulting game-playing programs without prescribing self-improvement algorithm.

sections.title: 3 Coding4Games Benchmark
sections.content: Coding4Games investigates whether modern coding agents can play video games by developing standalone executable programs. For each evaluation task, we specify game, an objective, starting scenario, and an interaction budget. Evaluating this capability requires both an environment for developing programs through game interaction and protocol for testing the resulting programs independently. We therefore introduce framework that connects sandboxed development environment to gym-like game server across diverse set of games while keeping program development separate from program evaluation. Below, we present the evaluation framework (Sec. 3.1), the games and their tasks (Sec. 3.2), and the measures used to score them (Sec. 3.3).

sections.title: 3.1 Evaluation framework
sections.content: As shown in Fig. 2, the framework makes heterogeneous games accessible to coding agents and evaluates the programs they produce under independent, consistent conditions. Given the input prompt of task description, API documentation, and setting description, the coding agent combines game server for standardized interaction, Development stage that supports autonomous software development, and an isolated Test stage for evaluating frozen programs. Below, we introduce the main components of the evaluation framework. Game Server. Games differ in how they start, expose observations, and accept inputs, making them difficult to access consistently from coding environment. The game server wraps each task with shared, gym-like interface for starting episodes, returning game screenshots, and applying gameplay inputs. It also tracks elapsed game tics and computes task-specific scores from gameplay evidence independently of the coding agent. Keeping initialization, game-tic accounting, and scoring under host control separates gameplay from measurement and supports fair, consistent evaluation across submitted programs. Development Stage. The Development stage gives coding agent one persistent sandbox for each development run, in which it can use real coding CLI to write, execute, and debug programs (OpenAI, 2025; Anthropic, 2025). Keeping this sandbox across iterations preserves the agents tools and intermediate work and reduces variation from changes in the development environment. The sandbox is configured to block direct access to game implementation files and the host-side scorer; game observation and control instead pass through the game servers MCP interface (Anthropic, 2024). The agent can repeatedly interact with the game, test and revise candidates, and select program artifact, Psel; it may 4 Figure 2 Evaluation framework. The game server provides common interface to heterogeneous games. Coding agents develop and select programs in sandbox; the frozen programs are then evaluated through independent rollouts with host-controlled initialization, budgets, and scoring. influence game outcomes through normal gameplay inputs, not by editing game files or scores. The host separately records model-token use and game tics, enforcing token budget, cumulative game-tic budget, and per-rollout game-tic limit that bound further interaction and determine when development must stop. Agent and game interactions, candidate tests, and resource use are logged as an auditable development trajectory. Together, the stable sandbox and recorded trajectory support reproducible experimental procedure without requiring identical gameplay outcomes. Test Stage. The Test stage evaluates the selected frozen program in fresh environment, separate from development (Jimenez et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2026). The program runs without model inference or public network access; its code stays fixed, although its internal state can change during play. Each test rollout follows the same per-rollout game-tic limit as development. Before each rollout, the host prepares the designated scenario using recorded initialization actions. After the rollout, the host-side scorer computes task-specific score from gameplay evidence. Repeated rollouts estimate the programs performance and variability under the same task conditions.

sections.content: Our evaluation includes 12 coding-agent models. sections.title: 4.1 Main results
sections.content: Overall performance. Table 3 shows substantial variation across models and games. Eight coding models achieve the highest coding score on at least one game: GPT-6-Astra leads on five, while Claude-Opus-5.5 leads on NBA 2K25 and Aimlab. Panel (a) on the left of Figure 3 also shows different category profiles, with GPT-5.6-Sol strongest in Combat & Action Timing and Claude-Opus-5.5 in 3D Sports & Precision Control. Even within category, no model consistently leads: GPT-6-Astra scores highest among coding agents on Balatro and Slay the Spire, whereas GPT-5.6-Sol leads on Kingdom Rush 5. The human player outperforms all agents on 10 of 15 games; GUI agents exceed this reference on Forza Horizon 5, and coding agents do so on Balatro, Forza Horizon 5, Slay the Spire, Riders Republic, and Aimlab. In the Computer Use Comparison, GPT-5.6-Sols frozen programs outperform its GUI baseline on eight games and underperform on seven; Claude-Sonnet-5s programs win on seven, lose on six, and tie on two. Together, these results show that strong performance remains specific to particular models and games, and that frozen programs offer an alternative to online GUI control whose relative effectiveness varies across tasks.

sections.title: 4.2 Understanding the performance
sections.content: 1. What strategies do agents implement? Models differ in how they use game information to control actions. Table 4 shows that GPT-5.6-Sol mainly produces G1 controllers, which select actions according to timing or counters. In contrast, GPT-6-Astra more often produces G3 programs that use game state to guide decisions, while G4 is the most common level for Claude Opus 5 and Qwen3.8-flash, indicating the use of memory, planning, and recovery alongside game state. These distributions distinguish programs that largely follow predefined schedules from those that adjust decisions using feedback and accumulated information. Coding agents therefore differ in the control logic they encode, although greater reliance on game state does not by itself establish better performance. 2. Do more complex strategies perform better? Greater strategy complexity does not necessarily yield higher 8 game performance. In Forza Horizon 5, Qwen3.8-flashs PID controller achieves mean score of 443.7, compared with 645.7 for Claude-Sonnet-5s simpler local route follower. Qwen3.8-flashs development traces record road departures and false recovery triggers, pointing to unresolved calibration issues, although their exact contribution to the score gap cannot be isolated. This gap between writing complex control code and calibrating it at runtime helps explain why stronger conventional programming performance may not transfer to standalone gameplay. 3. Do agents resolve failures through self-testing? Agents can identify problems during self-testing without reliably repairing them. Table 4 reports NER values ranging from 80.0% to 100%, but RS values spanning wider range from 35.7% to 83.3% for identified problems targeted by modifications. GPT-5.6-Sol and Gemini-3.8-flash achieve NER values of 100.0% and 94.4%, respectively, yet their RS values are 41.7% and 58.8%, respectively. Obtaining relevant test feedback therefore does not ensure successful repair. Moreover, local problem resolution still requires independent testing to establish improved game performance. 4. How do agents interact during debugging? Most models rely primarily on script execution to obtain feedback during development and debugging. Panel (b) on the left of Figure 3 shows that in the illustrated development runs, program execution accounts for most game tics for 10 of 12 models, reaching 98.5% for GPT-5.6-Sol. Direct interaction accounts for most game tics for Gemini-3.8-Flash (56.3%) and Kimi-K3 (65.3%). These shares characterize development interaction, but do not distinguish exploration from targeted debugging or measure log-inspection time. Unequal run counts and budgets also limit their interpretation as stable model preferences. 5. Where do frozen programs fail? Partial state representations limit how frozen programs adapt to feedback. In Riders Republic, GPT-5.6-Sols selected program detects crashes using red-screen threshold but executes tricks on fixed counter-based schedule. Feedback thus supports recovery without adapting trick selection or timing to the gameplay state: detecting failures alone is insufficient to guide the actions that precede them. 6. How do frozen programs compare with GUI agents? Frozen programs can match or exceed the same models GUI agent on some games without model inference during testing. Table 5 compares paired results for GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Sonnet-5. GPT-5.6-Sols programs score higher on eight of 15 paired games and lower on seven; Claude-Sonnet-5s programs score higher on seven, lower on six, and tie on two. Both models programs outperform their GUI agents on Balatro, Kingdom Rush 5, and KOF98, spanning strategy and combat tasks. However, both GUI agents score higher on Forza Horizon 5, Slay the Spire, Brotato, and Palworld. These results show that programs produced during development can support comparable or better gameplay on subset of tasks without continued model involvement, but they do not yet provide general replacement for online GUI-agent decision-making. 7. How do development budgets affect frozen-program performance? Both token and game-tic budgets influence performance, but their benefits vary across games. We examine how game-tic and token budgets affect test performance for Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6-Sol on Balatro, Black Myth: Wukong, and Forza Horizon 5 in the right panel of Fig. 3. We vary the cumulative game-tic budget from 5k to 15k in increments of 2k while fixing the token budget at 10 million, and vary the token budget from 5 to 25 million in increments of 3 million while fixing the game-tic budget at 10k.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced Coding4Games, benchmark that asks coding agents to develop standalone programs that play 15 modern games from visual observations through keyboard-and-mouse inputs, separating autonomous development in sandbox from independent, model-free testing of frozen program, and evaluating the development process alongside game performance and cost. Across 12 coding agents, the best program per game outscores the strongest GUI baseline on 13 of 15 games and ties it on one. The human player outscores all agents on 10 games. Our process measures reveal gap between self-testing and problem resolution: agents expose modifications to self-testing but often fail to resolve the failures they target, leaving programs that cover part of the gameplay conditions or rest on visual assumptions that do not hold outside the observed scenario. Turning execution feedback into revisions that generalize is, on this evidence, the central open problem for coding agents in dynamic environments.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: The research questions, hypotheses, and conceptual framework were developed by the authors without generative AI assistance. We used generative AI tools, primarily OpenAI Codex, to discuss and refine the methodology and to carry out most of the code implementation. AI tools also assisted with recording and analyzing experimental logs, analyzing and interpreting experimental results, conducting the literature survey, polishing the manuscript and generating visual materials, including background illustrations. The authors reviewed the entire manuscript and the outputs produced by the code, and rigorously tested the implementation against the intended requirements. The authors take responsibility for the final text, claims, results, and research artifacts, including those produced with AI assistance.
